Abstract Background  Achievement emotions play an important role in learning, significantly affecting well-being, learning satisfaction, and academic achievement, yet their application to healthcare education remains sparse. To address this gap, this study adapted the Achievement Emotions Questionnaire– Short Version (AEQ-S) in healthcare education. The objective is to assess the applicability, demonstrate its application, and guide future research in achievement emotions within this field. Methods  This study involved 296 pre-service students enrolled in interprofessional education (IPE) from various disciplines, including Chinese Medicine, Engineering, Law, Medicine, Nursing, Pharmacy, Speech and Hearing Sciences, and Social Work, who completed the adapted AEQ-S in IPE context (AEQ-SIPE) before and after the IPE. Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and multiple linear regression were employed to examine the acceptability of AEQ-S. Results  The 32-item AEQ-SIPE capturing eight emotions (hope, pride, enjoyment, anxiety, anger, shame, boredom, and hopelessness) yielded good model fit: CFI = 0.937, NFI = 0.904, IFI = 0.937, TLI = 0.928, RMSEA = 0.076) and high internal reliability (α = 0.90 to 0.96). Regression analyses indicated that the eight emotions accounted for a significant amount of variance in explaining well-being and achievement outcomes. Pride positively predicted satisfaction in life, positive affect, and learning satisfaction, while shame negatively predicted satisfaction in life but positively predicted positive and negative affect. Conclusion  This study highlights the critical importance of achievement emotions in healthcare education and confirms the AEQ-SIPE as a valid tool for exploring these emotions in IPE. It sets the stage for future research to further investigate and understand the role of achievement emotions in this context.

Achievement emotions in healthcare education: understanding the application of achievement emotions questionnaire

Introduction Theory and empirical data have established the link between students’ emotions in the classroom (e.g., enjoy­ ment, anxiety) and their achievement outcomes. In par­ ticular, evidence has shown that students who experience positive emotions achieve better, enjoy social relation­ ships, and even live longer [1]. Defined as “emotions tied directly to achievement activities or achievement out­ comes” [2, p.317], this construct is referred to as achieve­ ment emotion (AE), which has been linked with various important learning outcomes such as motivation [3], engagement [4], learning persistence [5], satisfaction [6], problem-solving ability [7], and learning and achieve­ ment [8]. These established relationships may be why the repeated calls made to explore non-cognitive constructs to account for factors in explaining students’ engagement and achievement in healthcare education [9]. However, despite such calls to action, AE studies in healthcare edu­ cation settings remain scant, and actionable plans for inducing adaptive emotions appear not to be in place (cf [10, 11, 12]).

One way to draw traction on this important construct is by providing researchers with psychometrically sound measures and guiding them in conceptualizing impor­ tant studies to advance academic emotion theory and application in healthcare education. The Achievement Emotions Questionnaire (AEQ) is a widely-known multidimensional tool and is considered one of the seminal research measures on students’ emotional experiences in educational settings [13]. Framed using the control-value theory of achievement emotion [14, 15], this theory pos­ its that achievement emotions arise from the interplay between control (students’ perceived ability to influence academic outcomes) and value (the perceived impor­ tance of the achievement situation). The AEQ operation­ alizes this theoretical framework by assessing students’ AEs underpinning three positive (pride, hope, and enjoy­ ment) and five negative emotions (anxiety, boredom, anger, shame, and hopelessness). Each emotion reflects specific control-value combinations (e.g., anxiety devel­ ops when students highly value performance but per­ ceive limited control over success) that impact learning outcomes and well-being in healthcare education set­ tings [13]. It has been translated into various language versions, including Japanese [16], Spanish [17], Chinese [18], German [19] and Korean [20]. From the original 80 items [13], an AEQ-Short Version (AEQ-S) has been formulated, requiring less time to administer and score [21, 22]. AEQ has also been applied in various contexts: sports [23], physics learning [24], mathematics educa­ tion [25], language learning [26], and teacher education

[27]. However, healthcare education environments pres­ ent distinctive characteristics that may intensify achieve­ ment emotions beyond these traditional academic and professional training settings, including direct patient care responsibilities, exposure to human suffering and mortality, ethical decision-making under pressure, and the professional obligation to maintain competence where errors have life-threatening consequences. These unique contextual factors create heightened emotional stakes and may influence the manifestation and inten­ sity of achievement emotions differently compared to other educational domains. Previous studies suggest that students often experience a wide spectrum of emotions throughout their learning processes [28], and these emo­ tions affect achievement gains [14] and satisfaction [20]. These learning-related emotions may recur periodically at various frequencies in various learning areas, including healthcare education [11, 12]. Studies have shown that positive emotions (e.g., pride, hope) are associated with higher satisfaction and well-being [29, 30]. Conversely, negative emotion, such as shame, arises from negative self-assessments, often triggered by perceived failures or shortcomings. It is typically linked to decreased life satisfaction and increased negative affect, as shame pro­ motes feelings of inadequacy and self-consciousness [31]. A study found that in Belgium, the prevalence of anger, boredom, anxiety, and shame was 15.6%, 7.2%, 4.7%, and 4.5%, respectively [32]. In Hong Kong, more than 50% of the 1,119 undergraduate students who were polled reported having anxiety symptoms [33]. From the lens of the control-value theory of academic emotion, these emotions are linked with students’ well-being [34], satis­ faction [35], and even academic performance in the long term [14]. Despite all these significances, the validation and application of AEQ-S in healthcare education, espe­ cially in Interprofessional education (IPE) context, are unexplored areas with significant potential for learning outcomes.

An adaptation and application of AEQ-S to healthcare education, particularly in IPE, is an important step that will eventually lead to the development of a research agenda to understand the mechanisms within which AEs translate into achievement gains. IPE is fast becoming one of the accreditation standards for healthcare pro­ fessions because of the relative benefits of a team-based interprofessional approach to care management. Accord­ ing to the World Health Organization [36], promoting IPE from the onset of healthcare education encourages adaptability and prepares students to meet complex healthcare needs more effectively. IPE in undergraduate healthcare curricula is envisioned to be a means by which

health professional students learn to increase efficacy in collaboration with one another [37] to achieve desirable benefits, including reduction of medical errors leading to topnotch quality of care [38, 39]. By situating our study within a Ten-Day IPE Programme, we aim to capture the various students’ AEs experienced and investigate their correlations with well-being and learning satisfaction.

The present study Although the AEQ-S is a well-established questionnaire, its application in the context of healthcare is still very limited. Therefore, the purpose of this study was three­ fold. First, we wanted to adapt the AEQ-S for estimating students’ AEs by adapting the items to the IPE context. Second, we aimed to conduct a confirmatory factor analy­ sis using the advantages of within-network approaches in examining construct validity. Finally, we sought to estab­ lish the relationship between AEs as measured by the AEQ-S in the IPE context (AEQ-SIPE) and other theo­ retically relevant constructs such as well-being (indexed by life satisfaction, positive and negative affect) and learning satisfaction. In this study, we hypothesized that the various AEs they feel across the period of complet­ ing the IPE activities with diverse discipline memberships would be linked with their well-being (satisfaction in life, positive affect, negative affect) and learning satisfaction (team learning satisfaction). The inclusion of positive affect and negative affect is grounded in the circumplex model of affect [40], which defines emotional experiences

along dimensions of valence and arousal. This framework complements Pekrun’s Control-Value Theory of Achieve­ ment Emotions [2], as positive affect and negative affect capture broader emotional tendencies that shape the like­ lihood of experiencing specific achievement emotions (e.g., enjoyment, anxiety). The study seeks to answer the following question: How do achievement emotions, as measured by the AEQ-SIPE, relate to well-being and learning satisfaction in the context of IPE among health­ care students? Finally, we propose research topics using the newly validated scale to help plan new directions for IPE research.

Method Participants and procedures There were 296 students from two institutions of higher learning participated in this study. The participants were from eight disciplines: Chinese Medicine (n = 16), Engi­ neering (n = 2), Law (n = 15), Medicine (n = 110), Nursing (n = 107), Pharmacy (n = 24), Speech and Hearing Sci­ ences (n = 4), and Social Work (n = 18). There were 43.2% males and 56.8% females, with an average age of 21.68 years (SD = 2.11).

Students participated in a required credit-bearing “Ten-Day Interprofessional Education” programme on COVID-19 Infection Control and Management (Fig. 1). The IPE programme integrates team-based and casebased learning pedagogies to enhance collaborative lead­ ership, problem-solving, conflict resolution, and clinical

reasoning skills. On Days 1–3, students engage online to build team identity (e-meet and name my team), review pre-class materials, and fill in a pre-evaluation survey. Days 4–9 involve face-to-face and online activities where students watch the case scenario, answer team-based questions, write team reflections, design interprofes­ sional healthcare plans for a COVID-19 patient case, facilitated by near-peer-teachers using constructive controversy. On Day 10, the programme culminates in an enrichment activity, where teams answer readiness assurance test, present their care plans for recognition of the best interprofessional care plans, engage in a whole class debriefing, and complete post and peer evaluation survey. While the rest of the disciplines were closely healthcare-related, the inclusion of Engineering and Law were especially important in the investigation of housing design, which may explain the spread of virus, and the legal issues arising from policy implementation.

Data were collected at the beginning (Days 1–3, base­ line measurement) and end of the IPE programme (Day 10, post-intervention measurement) through online questionnaires in the Qualtrics platform. All participants voluntarily signed an online consent form to fill out the questionnaires. There were no missing data in the dataset as all items in the Qualtrics online survey were required to be completed prior to survey submission.

Adaptation of achievement emotions questionnaire in IPE (AEQ-SIPE) Content experts in the IPE were asked to independently review the items of the proposed scale conducted in Eng­ lish for content validity based on the original scale pub­ lished by Pekrun et al. [41]. For example, “I enjoy being in class” was slightly modified to “I enjoy being in IPE” making it more context-specific. Due caution was exer­ cised in the context adaptation process, where our pri­ mary goal was to maintain the conceptual meaning of the items. Furthermore, we calculated internal consistency reliability using Cronbach’s alpha and split-half reliability coefficient. To validate the scales, we examined withinand between-network construct validity.

Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was conducted for within-network validation, and linear regression between the scales and external measures was used for betweennetwork validation, which functions similarly to criterion validity. Within-network construct validation is an exam­ ination of the factor structure, while the between-net­ work or external construct validation approach examines the relationships between the measures being validated and theoretical constructs [42]. We built from the litera­ ture and hypothesized that students’ AEs would be linked with their well-being (satisfaction with life, positive affect, negative affect). That is, students’ enjoyment (collected at

Time 1) will predict subsequent positive affect (collected at Time 2). CFA is part of structural equation modeling techniques, which enables the investigation of causal relations among latent and observed variables when the a priori model is specified [43]. This dual approach to scale validation has been popularly employed in validation studies and is thought to be robust [44]. It has also been used in healthcare education (e.g [45]).

Instruments Achievement Emotions Questionnaire - Short version in IPE (AEQ-SIPE). This study adapted the Achieve­ ment Emotions Questionnaire– short version [21]. The scale consists of 32 items divided into 8 subscales of 4 items each in the English version: enjoyment (4 items, “I enjoy participating so much in IPE that I get energized”; α = 0.96; split-half reliability coefficient = 0.94), hope (4 items, “I am full of hope”; α = 0.92; split-half reliability coefficient = 0.91), pride (4 items, “I am proud of myself”; α = 0.92; split-half reliability coefficient = 0.90), anger (4 items, “I am angry”; α = 0.94; split-half reliability coef­ ficient = 0.94), anxiety (4 items, “I feel nervous in IPE”; α = 0.90; split-half reliability coefficient = 0.87), shame (4 items, “I get embarrassed”; α = 0.95; split-half reliability coefficient = 0.95), hopelessness (4 items, “I feel hopeless”; α = 0.96; split-half reliability coefficient = 0.95), boredom (4 items, “I get bored”; α = 0.95; split-half reliability coef­ ficient = 0.94). To adapt the scale to IPE, the wording was slightly modified. For instance, the item “I enjoy being in class” was modified to “I enjoy being in IPE” (Appendix A). The scale is answerable from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).

Life Satisfaction Scale (LSS) and Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS- Short Form). We used these scales to measure students’ well-being, which was used in a previous study among Asian students [46]. Life sat­ isfaction was assessed using the Life Satisfaction Scale (5 items; e.g., “In most ways, my life is close to my ideal”, α = 0.95) from Diener et al. [47]. The response scale ranges from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). We also used the 10-item PANAS-Short Form, developed by MacKinnon et al. [48], to measure positive and nega­ tive affect. Participants were asked to score their feel­ ings of positive (e.g., “Interested”; α = 0.94) and negative (e.g., “Afraid”; α = 0.93) affect on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree; 5 = strongly agree).

Learning Satisfaction with Team Experience. We uti­ lized the subscale of the Students’ Team Experience Questionnaire to measure learning satisfaction with team experience [49]. This subscale is composed of five items (e.g., “I have found working as part of an IPE team in my classes to be a valuable experience”; α = 0.94), answerable from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).

Statistical analysis To establish within-network validity, we first conducted CFA using the Maximum Likelihood (ML) estimation method to examine the internal structure (within-net­ work construct validity) of the AEQ-SIPE using health­ care students’ data, which determined if our data would adequately fit the eight-factor structure [50]. Eight achievement emotions (e.g., enjoyment and anger, etc.) were conceptualized as latent variables, each represented by four observed indicators. We ensured the distribution normality of these indicators before applying ML esti­ mation, which is noted for its robustness and efficiency. Additionally, error covariances were introduced between closely related indicators (e.g., enjoyment and anger) to account for shared method-specific variance and improve model fit.We used the standard goodness-of-fit indices such as the root mean square error of approxima­ tion (RMSEA), standardized root means square residual (SRMR), comparative fit index (CFI), normed fit index (NFI), incremental fit index (IFI), and the Tucker-Lewis index (TLI) in evaluating the model fit. According to guidelines, all indices must be more than or equal to 0.90, except for RMSEA and SRMR, which must be less than or equal to 0.08 [51, 52, 53]. To further understand the data, we used an independent sample t-test to examine gender differences and multi-group CFA to check for measure­ ment invariance between genders using nested mod­ els [54]. In the nested models (configural model, metric model, and scalar model), we imposed constraints gradu­ ally. First, we used configural model which contains the same factor structure with fixed and free loadings calcu­ lated concurrently in the groups, but parameter estima­ tions were not subject to any between-groups restrictions

[55]. Then, we tested for measurement equivalence under the metric model by demanding that the factor structure and factor loadings be equivalent in the groups [56]. To further assess measurement equivalence using the sca­ lar model, a restriction is that the factor structure and loadings, covariance and variance should be equal in the groups [57].

To achieve the purpose of between-network valid­ ity, we used multiple regression analysis to clarify the relationship between each of the four dependent vari­ ables and the eight independent variables (the AEs). We used Statistical Package for Social Sciences for the t-test and regression (SPSS Version 27; [58]) and Analysis for Moment Structures for the CFA (AMOS 26; [59]).

Results Table 1 shows the basic statistics of the study variables. AEQ-SIPE has good internal consistency (from α = 0.90 to 0.96). Skewness (from − 0.59 to 0.76) and kurtosis (from − 0.41 to 0.92) were within the acceptable range [60].

Within-network construct validity According to Finney and DiStefano [60], univariate nor­ mality is not present when skewness and kurtosis abso­ lute values are more than 2 and 7, respectively. Our data, with skewness ranging from 0.24 to.76 and kurtosis rang­ ing from 0.04 to.92, matched the essential criteria for doing CFA. The results in Table 2 show that eight-latent factors obtained a good fit to our data: (χ² (df) = 1175.757 (436), CFI = 0.937, NFI = 0.904, IFI = 0.937, TLI = 0.928, RMSEA = 0.076). support the model’s psychometric acceptability in the IPE context. The final eight-factor AEQ-SIPE model is shown in Fig. 2.

The eight-factor model was tested for gender-specific invariance. As we executed multi-group CFA, we gradu­ ally restricted the models and computed the CFI decrease among the models (i.e., metric model, scalar model, and configural model). According to Cheung and Rensvold [57], the restricted parameters are invariant between groups if the CFI decreases by less than 0.01. As shown in Table 3, the results established gender invariance of the scale.

We also compared means to clarify if the eight-factor model could differentiate between participants’ scores in terms of gender. Results revealed that there were sig­ nificant gender differences in enjoyment (t(294) = 2.96, d = 0.97, p =.008), hopelessness (t(294)=-2.23, d = 1.05, p =.027), and boredom (t(294)=-2.26, d = 1.14 p =.024) with big effect sizes, while there was no other significant difference in hope, pride, anger, anxiety, and shame. Spe­ cifically, compared to males (M = 2.92, SD = 1.04), females (M = 3.23, SD = 0.92) registered higher mean scores in one positive emotion: enjoyment. In terms of negative emotions, hopelessness was lower for females (M = 2.00, SD = 0.96) than for males (M = 2.28, SD = 1.16), and bore­ dom was also lower for females (M = 2.49, SD = 1.10) than for males (M = 2.79, SD = 1.19) (see Table 4).

Between-network construct validity. To understand the between-network construct validity of the AEQ-SIPE, Table 5 revealed significant relationships among the study variables. Positive emotions, such as enjoyment, hope, and pride, were strongly positively correlated with satis­ faction in life (r =.551, r =.614, and r =.605, respectively, all p <.001), positive affect (r =.837, r = 759, and r =.810, respectively, all p <.001), and team learning satisfaction (r =.650, r =.731, and r =.757, respectively, all p <.001). In contrast, negative emotions, including hopelessness and boredom, showed significant negative correlations with satisfaction in life (r = −.179, p <.01; r = −.224, p <.001), positive affect (r = −.124, p <.01; r = −.379, p <.001), and team learning satisfaction (r = −.276, p <.001; r = −.252, p <.001).

We futher examined the link between achievement emotions as measured by AEQ-SIPE as a predictor of well-being and team learning satisfaction. The theoreti­ cal link between emotion and well-being [34] and learn­ ing satisfaction [6] has been established previously in other contexts. As shown in Table 6, satisfaction in life (F(8, 295) = 25.499, p <.001, R2 = 0.399), positive affect (F(8, 295) = 107.653, p <.001, R2 = 0.743), negative affect (F(8,295) = 78.429, p <.001, R2 = 0.677), and team learning satisfaction (F(8, 295) = 68.192, p <.001, R2 = 0.646) were significantly predicted by achievement emotions. Specifi­ cally, hope, pride, and shame predicted life satisfaction;

enjoyment, pride, and shame predicted positive affect. These results were consistent with our hypotheses.

Discussion This study aims to determine the construct validity of AEQ-SIPE and advance the conversation on achievement emotions in healthcare education by providing research­ ers with a scale to use in their investigation. The findings supporting the eight-factor structure of the AEQ-SIPE are consistent with previous validation studies, such as the original AEQ-S [21] and its Spanish-translated ver­ sion [17]. The findings further highlight that one can use the short version of the AEQ without sacrificing the structural model of the scale. Our study expands the application of AEQ-S to from individual to collaborative learning environments.

The results of within-network validity revealed that the eight-factor AEQ-S IPE structure obtained a good fit for our current data involving IPE students. Our results met the criteria of acceptable fit using various goodness-offit indices: CFI, NFI, IFI, TLI, RMSEA, and SRMR, sug­ gesting the internal validity of the scale. The results are consistent with previous work supporting AEQ among other samples, such as secondary school students [17] and university students [21]. Our findings reaffirm the factor structure established in prior AEQ validation stud­ ies, confirming the distinctiveness of positive and nega­ tive emotions like pride, enjoyment, shame, and anxiety. The consistency of these constructs across diverse educa­ tional settings highlights the context-independent valid­ ity of the AEQ.

Further, our results showed metric, scalar, configurar invariance providing good support for gender invari­ ance for the AEQ-SIPE eight-factor model. We then per­ formed t-tests to examine gender differences across the eight AEs. Results indicated that females in our sample had significantly higher enjoyment than males, while males were significantly higher in hopelessness and bore­ dom than females. These gender differences in AEs were consistent with the earlier studies in other contexts [19, 61, 62]. One possible reason is that male students are less emotionally invested in and enjoy academic activi­ ties, because they need to develop stronger interpersonal relationships with teachers to become more engaged in learning [63]. In addition, these differences may reflect gendered patterns in traditional gender role expectations and socialization. Traditionally, medicine (a predomi­ nantly male field) has been positioned above nursing and other care professions (predominantly female) in health­ care settings. These contradictory expectations require female students to be assertive and show enjoyment of collaboration to be effective team members. Meanwhile, male students’ higher levels of hopelessness and bore­ dom likely stem from gender socialization that values

individual competence and task orientation over the col­ laborative processes emphasized in IPE [64].

On the other hand, we also found some studies that are in contrast with our current findings. For example, a study among physical education students found that males had higher mean scores than females in terms of enjoyment while females had higher mean scores than males in terms of hopelessness and boredom [65]. In addition, a study among English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners also found that males had higher enjoy­ ment mean scores than females and females had higher hopelessness mean scores than males. In our results in the IPE context, one possible explanation is that per­ ceived gender norms can play a role on how Chinese students express their academic engagement and motiva­ tion [66, 67], and academic commitment [68]. Altogether, contrasting findings seem to exist in the literature regard­ ing gender differences in achievement emotions and our present findings add to this existing debate.

To establish the between-network validity, we con­ ducted correlation and regression analyses, which revealed a significant relationship between AEs and sub­ sequent well-being (life satisfaction and affect) and learn­ ing satisfaction. For example, pride positively predicted life satisfaction, positive affect, and learning satisfaction, while shame negatively predicted life satisfaction but pos­ itively predicted positive affect and negative affect. These findings are in general alignment with earlier studies [20, 69]. However, we also found non-significant relationships between some emotions and well-being and learning sat­ isfaction (e.g., anxiety and team learning satisfaction).

These non-significant results suggest that some emo­ tions may not directly impact well-being or learning satisfaction but could act through other mediators or moderators For example, previous study was found that the relationship between achievement emotions and aca­ demic achievement was moderated by academic buoy­ ancy [70]. Future research could explore these indirect pathways or environmental factors to gain a more com­ prehensive understanding of the role of emotions in education. Moreover, a counterintuitive finding of this study relates to boredom and shame, where contrary to our prediction, boredom positively predicted team learn­ ing satisfaction, and shame positively predicted positive affect. While we are surprised that this result requires further investigation, this may be explained by the speci­ fied beneficial effects of boredom or its different types [71] in some individuals under specific circumstances [72]. In IPE settings, boredom might serve a produc­ tive function by providing mental space for students to process complex interprofessional interactions, offering necessary mental breaks during intensive collaborative sessions where cognitive overload is common. Previous studies have suggested that boredom might not always directly enhance learning strategies [73], but can some­ times encourage individuals to seek new goals and expe­ riences [74]. Similarly, the positive correlation between shame and positive affect may appear unexpected. This relationship may reflect the distinctive learning dynam­ ics of IPE, where shame experienced after recognizing knowledge gaps about other professions’ roles can trigger heightened engagement and motivation to improve col­ laborative competencies. In healthcare education where professional identity formation is closely tied to com­ petency development, shame may function as a catalyst for professional growth when experienced in supportive interprofessional environments. Research indicates that certain negative emotions, like shame, can sometimes contribute to positive outcomes if they motivate individ­ uals to improve their performance or engage more deeply with the content to avoid future negative feelings [75]. Our initial results on the relationship between shame and outcomes require further investigation.

The observed gender differences in achievement emotions suggest adopting differentiated approaches, with male students benefiting from more interactive, hands-on activities during face-to-face sessions and gamified elements in online phases to enhance engage­ ment, while maintaining collaborative environments that support female students’ higher enjoyment levels. The unexpected positive relationships between certain nega­ tive emotions and learning outcomes indicate that educa­ tors should strategically channel emotions like boredom through varied case scenarios and competitive plan inte­ gration activities rather than eliminating them entirely. Finally, monitoring achievement emotions using the AEQ-SIPE at strategic points, such as at the early imple­ mentation phases, enables the early identification of atrisk students and facilitates targeted interventions. This approach creates an emotion-informed IPE design that progresses from self-directed learning through collabora­ tive application to reflective enrichment, which enhance student engagement, learning satisfaction, and profes­ sional development outcomes.

Limitations Although this study has merits, it also has limitations that open up new research directions. First, although self-report measures are frequently used to collect data for confirmatory research due to their ease of use and data collection efficiency, this restriction raises the possibility of method bias [77]. Future studies could incorporate multiple data sources, such as behavioral observations to triangulate findings and enhance validity. Second, although eight different disciplines were included in the study, the sampling area was only in Hong Kong, and the sample size was not very large. Additionally, due to the challenges in participant recruitment result­ ing in the unbalanced distribution of participants across healthcare disciplines, with medical and nursing students comprising 73% of the sample while some disciplines had minimal representation (engineering n = 2, speech and hearing sciences n = 4), may limit the generalizability of findings across all healthcare fields. The smaller sample sizes in certain disciplines preclude meaningful subgroup analyses and may not fully capture discipline-specific achievement emotion patterns. Given that medical and nursing programs typically involve high-intensity clini­ cal training, the current findings may be most represen­ tative of achievement emotions in intensive healthcare education contexts. Future research would benefit from more balanced recruitment across healthcare disciplines

Third, our study used cross-sectional data which captured a ‘snapshot’ of the study variables in one time-point. Future studies can use longitudinal research design to establish causal relation­ ships among the study variables. Fourth, the relationship among the study variables is only through correlation and regression. Further studies can incorporate media­ tion analysis to further investigate the pathways linking emotions to outcomes through intermediate variables. Finally, the effect of emotions was examined in a single IPE programme on COVID-19 Infection Control and Management. Further studies can consider collect­ ing data from AEQ-SIPE and AEQ-S in different IPE programmes.

Conclusion By and large, we are excited about the newly validated AEQ-SIPE, as this signals a great opportunity for health professional education researchers to contribute to mov­ ing the healthcare education literature forward. Theoreti­ cally, this study provides researchers with the impetus to investigate the relationship between subjective feel­ ings and other variables in the setting of IPE. Practically, this study proposes several potential research topics for researchers to maximize the use of the newly validated tool to contribute to further elucidating the role of AEs in achieving outcomes in the IPE context (Table 7). There­ fore, we propose utilizing AEQ-SIPE to develop mean­ ingful research agendas in IPE.
